messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Electrician
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 33

I sit across from Mr. Aris Thakur, seventy-six, his hands resting on his knees like two old tools waiting for a job. The afternoon light catches the silver in his mustache as he talks about the alley behind the old textile factory. He never uses the word trauma. He calls it the Tuesday the world went dark. He describes the alley as if it were happening now. He walks home from a late shift, his tool belt heavy against his hips, the familiar weight of pliers and wire strippers settling into his palms. A young man steps from the shadows, a knife catching the streetlight like a stripped copper wire. Aris remembers the smell of diesel and wet pavement, the sharp command, the sudden collapse of his own body against the ground. He hands over his wallet, his watch, the leather pouch where he keeps his mother’s prayer beads. When the man runs, Aris lies still long enough to count the cracks in the asphalt, then stands, brushes off his trousers, and walks the rest of the way home. The quiet never returned. At first, it is the dreams. He wakes at 3 a.m., heart hammering against his ribs, fingers curling as if gripping something that isn’t there. Meera, his wife of forty-two years, learns to sleep with the hall light on. She touches his shoulder when he jolts, but he flinches before he realizes it’s her. He stops carrying his wallet in his front pocket. He measures every streetlamp by its distance from his house. He tells himself he is being careful, a sensible old man, but I watch his eyes scan the room every time the clinic door clicks shut. Before the alley, Aris was known for his steady hands. Forty years running current through buildings, splicing wires with surgical patience, teaching apprentices how to read the color codes like a language. He used to say a good electrician never works in the dark. Now, the dark has a voice. It whispers in the static of dead circuits. He still drives his van, still checks grounding before he climbs the ladder, but he takes the long way around every construction site, every narrow passage. He tells me that when he holds a voltage tester, his thumb hovers over the metal tip, afraid it might spark the memory again. He misses the certainty of a closed loop. He misses knowing that if you follow the right wire, the light comes on. Meera tries to keep him busy with garden work, with grandsons who leave muddy footprints on the porch, with the quiet rituals of Sunday chai. She notices when he stops halfway down the sidewalk, eyes fixed on a parked car or a shadowed doorway. He doesn’t want to worry her, so he laughs it off, says his nerves are just tired. But his sleep is fractured, his coffee tastes like ash, and he flinches when a door slams in the building. He says he feels like a fuse that has blown—still in the wall, still connected, but no longer carrying the charge. He watches the young electricians at the union hall, their easy chatter, their unguarded strides, and wonders how they sleep through the night. He leans forward now, fingers tracing the edge of his chair. The afternoon stretches out, and for a moment, the clinic feels very quiet, very open. He breathes in, then out, and tells me he thinks he will walk home the same way tomorrow. I watch his shoulders rise and fall, the old craftsman still present beneath the watchfulness, waiting for the next spark, the next current, the next step into the light.
